title: Design of Experiments with Several Factors
summary: Chapter 7 varied one factor. Real processes depend on many factors, and the effect of one factor often depends on the level of another. The one-factor-at-a-time strategy cannot detect this, and it uses the data inefficiently. In a factorial experiment, all…

blocks.x: Chapter 7 varied one factor. Real processes depend on many factors, and the effect of one factor often depends on the level of another.
The one-factor-at-a-time strategy cannot detect this, and it uses the data inefficiently.
In a factorial experiment, all combinations of the levels of all factors are run. Each observation then helps estimate every effect.

sections.title: Some Applications of Designed Experiments (CD Only)

blocks.x: Factorial and fractional factorial designs are used to:
screen many factors for the few that matter;
characterise a process (find the settings and interactions that set the response);
optimise it (response surface methods);
establish robustness (find settings where the response is insensitive to noise factors such as temperature or operator).
Typical uses: chemical yield studies, tuning machining parameters, reliability testing, software configuration testing.
The main effect of a factor is the change in the mean response caused by changing that factor’s level, averaged over the levels of the other factors.
There is an interaction between two factors if the effect of one depends on the level of the other.
Two factors A and B at two levels each. Mean responses: at B low, A low $=10$ and A high $=20$. At B high, A low $=12$ and A high $=14$.
The effect of A is $+10$ at low B, but only $+2$ at high B. So A and B interact.
The average (main) effect of A is $6$. This misrepresents both situations.
Plot the means against the levels of A, one line per level of B. The lines are not parallel. Parallel lines mean no interaction.

For two factors at two levels, effects are differences of averages. Take the textbook’s Table 14-1: $A_{\text{low}}$ gives $10$ ($B_{\text{low}}$) and $20$ ($B_{\text{high}}$); $A_{\text{high}}$ gives $30$ and $40$. Then
The interaction effect is the difference of the diagonal averages. The lines of response against $A$ are parallel.
Now change the $B_{\text{high}}$, $A_{\text{high}}$ response to $0$ (Table 14-2: $10,20$ and $30,0$).
The $A$ effect is $30-10=20$ at $B_{\text{low}}$ and $0-20=-20$ at $B_{\text{high}}$.
The main effect of $A$ is $(30+0)/2-(10+20)/2=0$. This wrongly suggests $A$ does nothing.
The interaction is large: $AB=(10+0)/2-(20+30)/2=-20$.
A significant interaction can hide the main effects. Then knowing the interaction is more useful than knowing the main effects.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: why not one factor at a time?

blocks.x: A chemist fixes temperature at $155^\circ$F and varies time ($0.5$ to $2.5$ h). The best yield is near $1.7$ h. Then time is fixed at $1.7$ h and temperature varied ($140$ to $180^\circ$F). The best is near $155^\circ$F.

The conclusion “$155^\circ$F and $1.7$ h” can be at least $20$ yield points below the true optimum, which lies at shorter times and higher temperatures. The method fails because it cannot see the time–temperature interaction. A factorial experiment can. It also needs fewer runs.

blocks.caption: Interaction plots: one line per level of the second factor. Non-parallel lines indicate interaction.

blocks.x: Statistical Analysis of the Fixed-Effects Model
Factor A has $a$ levels and factor B has $b$ levels. Each of the $ab$ combinations is replicated $n$ times, in random order.
Y_{ijk}=\mu+\tau_i+\beta_j+(\tau\beta)_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ijk},\qquad i=1,\dots,a;\ j=1,\dots,b;\ k=1,\dots,n.
$\sum\tau_i=\sum\beta_j=0$.
$\sum_i(\tau\beta)_{ij}=\sum_j(\tau\beta)_{ij}=0$.
$\varepsilon_{ijk}\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2)$, independent.

Let $\bar{y}_{ij\cdot}$ be cell means, $\bar{y}_{i\cdot\cdot}$ row means, $\bar{y}_{\cdot j\cdot}$ column means and $\bar{y}_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}$ the grand mean. Then $SS_T=SS_A+SS_B+SS_{AB}+SS_E$, where
The degrees of freedom add as $abn-1=(a-1)+(b-1)+(a-1)(b-1)+ab(n-1)$.
Each ratio $F_A=MS_A/MS_E$, $F_B=MS_B/MS_E$, $F_{AB}=MS_{AB}/MS_E$ has an $F$ distribution under its null hypothesis.
Nulls: all $\tau_i=0$; all $\beta_j=0$; all $(\tau\beta)_{ij}=0$.
Numerator degrees of freedom: $a-1$, $b-1$, $(a-1)(b-1)$.
Denominator degrees of freedom: $ab(n-1)$.
Reject each null in the upper tail.
Computing formulas:

\begin{aligned}
SS_T&=\sum y_{ijk}^2-\frac{y_{\cdots}^2}{abn},\\
SS_A&=\frac1{bn}\sum y_{i\cdot\cdot}^2-\frac{y_{\cdots}^2}{abn},\\
SS_B&=\frac1{an}\sum y_{\cdot j\cdot}^2-\frac{y_{\cdots}^2}{abn},\\
SS_{AB}&=\frac1n\sum\sum y_{ij\cdot}^2-\frac{y_{\cdots}^2}{abn}-SS_A-SS_B,\\
SS_E&=SS_T-SS_{AB}-SS_A-SS_B.
\end{aligned}
Test the interaction first, then the main effects.
Factor A has $2$ levels, factor B has $3$, and $n=2$:
Both main effects and the interaction are significant.

Three primer types and two application methods (dipping, spraying), $n=3$ specimens per cell. Cell totals: primer 1 dip $12.8$, spray $15.9$; primer 2 $15.9$, $18.2$; primer 3 $11.5$, $15.5$. The grand total is $89.8$ over $18$ observations.
$SS_T=10.72$, $SS_{\text{types}}=4.58$, $SS_{\text{methods}}=4.91$, $SS_{\text{interaction}}=0.24$. By subtraction $SS_E=0.99$, with $12$ degrees of freedom ($MS_E=0.08$).
$f_{AB}=0.12/0.08=1.50<3.89$ ($P=0.262$). No evidence of interaction. The interaction plot has nearly parallel lines.

Spraying gives higher adhesion, and primer 2 the highest. With no interaction, compare the primer row averages (for example by Fisher’s LSD, as in Chapter 7). If the interaction were significant, compare the means of one factor with the other factor held at a fixed level.
If the interaction is significant, the main effects of A and B cannot be read separately. The effect of A depends on B.
In Example 8.6, the A effect grows from $+1$ at B1 to $+8$ at B3.
Compare the cell means (an interaction plot), not the marginal means.
Make multiple comparisons among cell means, at fixed levels of the other factor.
If the interaction is not significant, report the main effects and compare marginal means with Tukey’s method.
Model Adequacy Checking
The residuals are $e_{ijk}=y_{ijk}-\bar{y}_{ij\cdot}$. Check them as in Chapter 7:
a normal probability plot;
residuals against fitted values $\bar{y}_{ij\cdot}$ (the spread should be equal across cells);
residuals against factor levels and against run order.
Unequal variances across cells are the most damaging violation. If the spread depends on the mean, transform the response.
One Observation Per Cell
With $n=1$ there is no replication. $SS_E$ in the model above is zero, and the interaction cannot be separated from error.
If it is reasonable to assume no interaction:
use $SS_{AB}$ (with $(a-1)(b-1)$ df) as the error sum of squares;
test with $F_A=MS_A/MS_{AB}$ and $F_B=MS_B/MS_{AB}$.
This is the randomized block analysis of Chapter 7, with the second factor playing the role of blocks. Tukey’s one-degree-of-freedom test for nonadditivity checks the no-interaction assumption.
Factorial Experiments with Random Factors: Overview
If a factor is random (its levels are a random sample), its effects are random and the $F$-ratios change.
Both A and B random:
So $F_A=MS_A/MS_{AB}$ and $F_B=MS_B/MS_{AB}$. The interaction mean square is the denominator.
$F_{AB}=MS_{AB}/MS_E$.
Variance components come from solving these equations, for example $\hat\sigma_\tau^2=(MS_A-MS_{AB})/bn$.
Mixed model (A fixed, B random): the test for A uses $MS_{AB}$, and the test for B uses $MS_E$.
Rule: form each $F$-ratio so that numerator and denominator have the same expected value under the null hypothesis.
For factors A, B, C with $a,b,c$ levels and $n$ replicates, the model has three main effects, three two-factor interactions $AB,AC,BC$, and the three-factor interaction $ABC$:
Y_{ijkl}=\mu+\tau_i+\beta_j+\gamma_k+(\tau\beta)_{ij}+(\tau\gamma)_{ik}+(\beta\gamma)_{jk}+(\tau\beta\gamma)_{ijk}+\varepsilon_{ijkl}.
The analysis extends the two-factor case.
Each sum of squares comes from the matching marginal totals.
For fixed effects, $F=MS_{\text{effect}}/MS_E$.
Higher-order interactions are rarely large. Test the highest-order interaction first.
At least two replicates ($n\ge2$) are needed to compute $SS_E$.

Feed rate (A), depth of cut (B) and tool angle (C), each at two levels, with $n=2$. That gives $16$ observations and $8$ error degrees of freedom. The critical value for every effect is $f_{0.05,1,8}=5.32$.
Feed rate has a strong main effect.
Depth of cut has $P=0.0710$. Only suggestive.
The next largest effect is the $AB$ (feed $\times$ depth) interaction.
Both feed rate and depth of cut are probably important process variables.
The number of runs $abc\,n$ grows fast with the number of factors. This motivates the $2^k$ designs.

sections.title: Factorial Experiments with Random Factors (CD Only)

blocks.x: For random factors, the expected mean squares in the general model decide the test statistics, as in the two-factor case.
Each effect is tested against the mean square whose expectation has the same variance components under the null.
Sometimes no single mean square fits. Then use a linear combination of mean squares (Satterthwaite’s approximation), with approximate degrees of freedom.

The ANOVA table uses the same sums of squares as for fixed effects. Only the denominators of the $F$-ratios change, and the aim becomes estimating variance components rather than comparing level means.
When each of $k$ factors has just two levels (“low” $-$ and “high” $+$), the full factorial has $2^k$ runs per replicate. These designs are the workhorse of screening.
The $2^2$ Design
With factors A and B the four treatment combinations are:
$(1)$: both low;
$a$: A high, B low;
$b$: A low, B high;
$ab$: both high.
The same symbol also stands for the total of the $n$ observations at that combination.
A=\frac1{2n}\big[ab+a-b-(1)\big],\quad B=\frac1{2n}\big[ab+b-a-(1)\big],\quad AB=\frac1{2n}\big[ab+(1)-a-b\big].
The bracket is the effect’s contrast $C$. Each effect has one degree of freedom and $SS=C^2/(4n)$.
Also $SS_T=\sum\sum\sum y^2-y_{\cdot\cdot\cdot}^2/(4n)$ and $SS_E=SS_T-SS_A-SS_B-SS_{AB}$, with $4(n-1)$ degrees of freedom.
The coefficients of the contrasts form the sign table. Each effect is the average response where its sign is $+$ minus the average where it is $-$.
The main effects are significant. The interaction is not.
A $2^2$ design with $n=4$: deposition time (A) and arsenic flow rate (B). The response is layer thickness in $\mu$m.
Changing deposition time from low to high changes the mean thickness by $0.836\,\mu$m. B and AB are small.
The ANOVA confirms that only deposition time is significant.
The fitted model is $\hat{y}=\bar{y}+\tfrac12(0.836)x_1$ with $x_1=\pm1$. Residuals are $y-\hat{y}$ at each run. One large residual flags a possible outlier.
Facts to remember:
In a $2^k$ design, the square of the software’s $t$-statistic for an effect equals that effect’s $F$-ratio ($t^2=F$, on $1$ and $2^k(n-1)$ df).
The design is orthogonal, so sequential and adjusted sums of squares coincide.

Regression view. Code the factors $x_A,x_B=\pm1$. Then $\hat{y}=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_Ax_A+\hat\beta_Bx_B+\hat\beta_{AB}x_Ax_B$, with $\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}$. Each coefficient is half the effect, because $x$ moves by $2$ units from $-1$ to $+1$.
The columns are orthogonal, so the estimates are uncorrelated and each has variance $\sigma^2/(4n)$.
The $2^k$ Design for $k\ge3$ Factors
For $k=3$ there are $8$ combinations: $(1),a,b,ab,c,ac,bc,abc$. The seven effects are $A,B,C,AB,AC,BC,ABC$.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Effects and sums of squares in the $2^k$ design

blocks.x: Let $C$ be an effect’s contrast: the signed sum of treatment totals, with signs from the sign table. (A letter gets $+$ if the factor is high. Interaction signs are products.) Then
\text{effect}=\frac{C}{2^{k-1}n},\qquad SS=\frac{C^2}{2^kn},\qquad\text{each with one degree of freedom.}
The regression coefficient is half the effect. Total degrees of freedom: $2^kn-1=(2^k-1)+2^k(n-1)$.
Example: the A effect in $2^3$ is $\dfrac1{4n}\big[a+ab+ac+abc-(1)-b-c-bc\big]$.
The columns of the sign table are orthogonal. So each effect is estimated independently, with equal precision, and the sums of squares add up to $SS_T-SS_E$.
Single Replicate of the $2^k$ Design
The number of runs grows as $2^k$. For $k\ge4$ one often runs a single replicate ($n=1$). Then there are no degrees of freedom for error. Two fixes:

Normal probability plot of the effects. Effects of inactive factors are random draws from one normal distribution, so they fall on a straight line. Active effects stand off the line. No estimate of $\sigma$ is needed.
Pooling. By the sparsity of effects principle, high-order interactions (three-factor and above) are usually negligible. Pool their sums of squares into an error estimate and $F$-test the rest.
Then refit with only the significant terms and check the residuals.

Projection. Dropping $h$ negligible factors from a $2^k$ design with $n$ replicates leaves a $2^{k-h}$ design with $n2^h$ replicates. Dropping factor $C$ collapses the cube onto a square, with each corner run twice as often.
Counting effects: a $2^4$ has $4$ main effects, $6$ two-factor, $4$ three-factor and $1$ four-factor interaction. A $2^6$ has $6,15,20,15,6,1$.
Addition of Center Points to a $2^k$ Design (CD Only)
Add $n_C$ replicated runs at the center point ($x_i=0$ for all factors). They give:
an estimate of pure error from the center runs;
a test for curvature. If the true response is a plane, the center average equals the average of the factorial runs.
Let $\bar{y}_F$ be the mean of the $n_F$ factorial runs and $\bar{y}_C$ the mean of the $n_C$ center runs. Then
SS_{\text{curvature}}=\frac{n_Fn_C(\bar{y}_F-\bar{y}_C)^2}{n_F+n_C},\qquad F_0=\frac{SS_{\text{curvature}}}{MS_E}\quad(1,\ n_C-1\text{ df}),

where $MS_E$ is the pure-error variance from the center runs. A significant value means the linear model is inadequate and quadratic terms are needed. Center points do not disturb the estimates of main effects and interactions.

sections.title: Blocking and Confounding in the $2^k$ Design

blocks.x: A full replicate of $2^k$ may be too large for one homogeneous block (one batch of raw material, one day of production). Confounding splits it into smaller blocks. It deliberately makes one effect, usually the highest-order interaction, indistinguishable from the block difference.
That effect is sacrificed.
All other effects are estimated free of block differences.
To confound an effect, for example $ABC$ in a $2^3$, let $L=x_1+x_2+x_3$, where $x_i=0$ (low) or $1$ (high). Put runs with $L\equiv0\pmod2$ in one block, and runs with $L\equiv1\pmod2$ in the other.
$2^3$ confounded with $ABC$.
Block 1: $(1),\ ab,\ ac,\ bc$ (an even number of high factors).
Block 2: $a,\ b,\ c,\ abc$.
Every main-effect and two-factor contrast has two $+$ and two $-$ in each block, so the block difference cancels.
The $ABC$ contrast is $+$ for all of block 2 and $-$ for all of block 1. It cannot be separated from the block effect.
If $ABC$ is negligible, as is usual, nothing of value is lost.
More blocks. Confound several effects.
With four blocks, choose two defining effects, say $AB$ and $AC$. Their product mod 2, $BC$, is confounded too (the generalised interaction). Three effects are lost.
In general, $2^p$ blocks need $p$ independent confounded effects and sacrifice $2^p-1$ effects.

Construction: with $L=\alpha_1x_1+\dots+\alpha_kx_k\pmod2$ (where $x_i\in\{0,1\}$ is the level of factor $i$ and $\alpha_i$ its exponent in the confounded effect), runs with the same $L$ go in the same block.
The block containing $(1)$ is the principal block. Get the other by multiplying one of its elements into each element of the principal block, mod 2 on the exponents.

For a $2^2$ with $AB$ confounded, the blocks are $\{(1),ab\}$ and $\{a,b\}$. $A$ and $B$ are unaffected, since each contrast has one plus and one minus run in each block. The block effect and $AB$ are identical.

In the textbook’s missile example, a $2^4$ is run in two blocks (two gunners) with $ABCD$ confounded. The three-factor interactions are pooled as error. Target type (A), target range (D) and the $AC$ and $AD$ interactions are large.
Partial confounding. Replicate the design with a different effect confounded in each replicate. Then every effect is estimable from some replicates.
Even a single replicate may be too costly when $k$ is large ($2^7=128$ runs). High-order interactions are usually negligible, so we can run only a fraction.
One-Half Fraction of the $2^k$ Design
Take the runs of the $2^3$ for which $ABC$ is $+$: $a,b,c,abc$. This is the principal fraction of a $2^{3-1}$ design, with defining relation $I=ABC$.

Two effects are aliases if their contrasts are identical in the fraction, so they cannot be separated. Find aliases by multiplying the effect by the defining relation, with $A^2=B^2=C^2=I$ (powers reduce mod 2).
For $I=ABC$: $A\cdot ABC=BC$, so $A=BC$. Likewise $B=AC$ and $C=AB$.
The estimate of “A” is really an estimate of $A+BC$. If $BC$ is negligible, it estimates $A$.
The complementary fraction $I=-ABC$ (runs $(1),ab,ac,bc$) estimates $A-BC$, and so on.
Running both recovers the full factorial. The sum and difference separate the aliases.
The resolution of a fractional design is the length of the shortest word in its defining relation.
Resolution III (for example $2^{3-1}_{\mathrm{III}}$, $I=ABC$): main effects are aliased with two-factor interactions.
Resolution IV (for example $2^{4-1}_{\mathrm{IV}}$, $I=ABCD$): main effects are clear of two-factor interactions. Two-factor interactions are aliased with each other ($AB=CD$).
Resolution V: main effects and two-factor interactions are clear of each other. They are aliased only with three-factor and higher.
A $2^{4-1}_{\mathrm{IV}}$ design (eight runs) with $I=ABCD$.
Aliases: $A=BCD$, $B=ACD$, $C=ABD$, $D=ABC$, $AB=CD$, $AC=BD$, $AD=BC$.
Construction: write the full $2^3$ in A, B, C and set $D=ABC$ (multiply the signs).
Four factors are studied in half the runs. Main effects are estimable if three-factor interactions are negligible.
Textbook examples:
Plasma etch. The $2^{4-1}$ with $I=ABCD$ shows large $A$ (gap), $D$ (power) and $AD$ effects, agreeing with the full factorial. Dropping $B$ and $C$ leaves a replicated $2^2$ in $A$ and $D$.
Unresolved aliases. Run the alternate fraction ($I=-ABC$) and combine. With $\ell$ and $\ell'$ the two estimates, $\tfrac12(\ell+\ell')$ estimates $A$ and $\tfrac12(\ell-\ell')$ estimates $BC$.
Bad generator. Choosing $I=AB$ in a $2^{3-1}$ aliases two main effects and loses important information.

Injection molding. A $2^{6-2}$ design (16 runs) shows large $A$ (mold temperature), $B$ (screw speed) and $AB$. Residuals against holding time $C$ show less scatter at low $C$. That points to a setting that reduces variability.
Three principles justify fractions:
Sparsity of effects: few effects are large.
Hierarchy: main effects matter more than two-factor interactions, which matter more than three-factor interactions.
Projection: a resolution $R$ design projects onto a full factorial in any $R-1$ factors.
If one factor is inactive, the $2^{4-1}$ collapses to a full $2^3$ in the others. No information is wasted.
Smaller Fractions: The $2^{k-p}$ Fractional Factorial
A $2^{k-p}$ design has $2^{k-p}$ runs, a $1/2^p$ fraction.
Start from a full $2^{k-p}$ design in $k-p$ basic factors.
Assign the other $p$ factors to interactions of the basic factors, using $p$ independent generators.
The defining relation holds the $p$ generator words and all their $2^p-1$ products.
Each effect has $2^p-1$ aliases. The resolution is the length of the shortest word in the complete defining relation.
Start from a $2^4$ in $A,B,C,D$, with generators $E=ABC$ and $F=BCD$. So $I=ABCE=BCDF$. Multiplying, $ABCE\cdot BCDF=ADEF$. The full relation is $I=ABCE=BCDF=ADEF$.
The shortest word has $4$ letters, so this is resolution IV.
Main effects are aliased with three-factor interactions, for example $A=BCE=DEF=ABCDF$.
Two-factor interactions are aliased with each other: $AB=CE$, $AC=BE$, $AD=EF$, $AF=DE$, …
Other designs:
$2^{7-3}_{\mathrm{IV}}$ (16 runs): $E=ABC$, $F=BCD$, $G=ACD$, with $I=ABCE=BCDF=ADEF=ACDG=BDEG=CEFG=ABFG$.

$2^{7-4}_{\mathrm{III}}$ (eight runs for seven factors): generators $D=AB$, $E=AC$, $F=BC$, $G=ABC$. It is saturated: all seven degrees of freedom estimate main effects. Its $15$-word defining relation includes $ABD=ACE=BCF=ABCG$ and their products.
Practical advice:
Choose generators to maximise the resolution. Tables of best designs exist.
Resolution III is for pure screening (assume interactions are negligible). Use resolution IV or V when interactions matter.
Foldover (run the design again with all signs reversed) breaks the aliasing of main effects with two-factor interactions. It turns resolution III into resolution IV.
Use fractions sequentially: begin with a small screening fraction, then add runs to resolve ambiguities.

sections.title: Response Surface Methods and Designs (CD Only)

blocks.x: Once the important factors are known, the goal is often to find the settings that optimise the response. Response surface methodology (RSM) fits a low-order polynomial in the coded factors and moves toward the optimum.
Steepest ascent. Far from the optimum, a first-order model $\hat{y}=\hat\beta_0+\sum\hat\beta_ix_i$ (from a $2^k$ with center points) is adequate.
The gradient $(\hat\beta_1,\dots,\hat\beta_k)$ gives the path of steepest ascent (descent, for a minimum).
Run experiments along it until the response stops improving. Then repeat with a new factorial centred there.

Second-order model. Near the optimum, curvature appears (center-point test). Fit $\hat{y}=\hat\beta_0+\sum\hat\beta_ix_i+\sum\hat\beta_{ii}x_i^2+\sum_{icentral composite design (CCD) adds $2k$ axial points $(\pm\alpha,0,\dots,0),\dots$ and center runs to a $2^k$ factorial. The Box–Behnken design is an alternative.

Canonical analysis. Write $\hat{y}=\hat\beta_0+\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{x}\T\hat{B}\mathbf{x}$. The stationary point is $\mathbf{x}_s=-\tfrac12\hat{B}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$. The eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix $\hat{B}$ classify it: all negative, a maximum; all positive, a minimum; mixed signs, a saddle (Linear Algebra, Chapter 16).
Factorial designs vary all factors together. They estimate main effects and interactions efficiently. If an interaction is significant, interpret cell means, not marginal means.

Two-factor ANOVA: $SS_T=SS_A+SS_B+SS_{AB}+SS_E$, with df $a-1$, $b-1$, $(a-1)(b-1)$, $ab(n-1)$. Fixed effects are tested against $MS_E$. One observation per cell requires assuming no interaction. For random factors, choose denominators from the expected mean squares.

$2^k$: effect $=C/(2^{k-1}n)$, $SS=C^2/(2^kn)$, regression coefficient $=$ half the effect. Single replicates use normal plots of effects or pooled high-order interactions. Center points test curvature.
Blocking by confounding sacrifices high-order interactions (for example $ABC$ in two blocks). Generalised interactions are confounded too.
Fractions $2^{k-p}$ use defining relations. Find aliases by multiplying. Resolution III/IV/V says which effects are aliased. Foldover and sequential experiments resolve ambiguities.
Response surface methods: steepest ascent, central composite designs, canonical analysis.

Analyse the following two-factor experiment ($a=3$, $b=2$, $n=2$): A1B1: $8,10$; A1B2: $12,14$; A2B1: $9,11$; A2B2: $20,22$; A3B1: $10,12$; A3B2: $15,17$. Construct the ANOVA table, test for interaction and main effects at $\alpha=0.05$, and draw the interaction plot.
In a $2^2$ design with $n=2$: $(1)=\{20,22\}$, $a=\{30,34\}$, $b=\{18,20\}$, $ab=\{28,32\}$. Compute the three effects, their sums of squares, the ANOVA table and the fitted regression equation.
Write the contrast for the effect $AC$ in a $2^3$ design and verify that it is orthogonal to the contrast for $B$.
Show that in a $2^k$ design with $n$ replicates each effect estimate has variance $\sigma^2/(2^{k-2}n)$, and that the regression coefficient has variance $\sigma^2/(2^kn)$.
Design a $2^3$ experiment in two blocks of four runs confounding $ABC$, and one in four blocks of two runs confounding $AB$ and $AC$; list the blocks and the confounded effects.
For a $2^{5-1}$ design with $I=ABCDE$, find the resolution, the aliases of $A$ and of $AB$, and explain what can be estimated if three-factor and higher interactions are negligible.
Construct the eight runs of the $2^{4-1}$ design with $D=ABC$, list the aliases of every main effect and two-factor interaction, and say why it is called resolution IV.

A first-order fit from a $2^2$ design with center points is $\hat{y}=50+3x_1-1.5x_2$ (coded units). Give the direction of steepest ascent and the coordinates of the first three points along it with step $\Delta x_1=1$.
